Lessons.Title: Equal Groups, Larger Numbers
ExplanationParagraphs: Original Which One Doesn't Belong? compares four distinct representations. Source A is a full7×14 grid, area98. B divides a7×13 rectangle into widths10 and3, with areas70+21=91. C divides7×14 into widths10 and4 labelled70+28=98 but image halves appear EQUAL in width—geometrically incorrect scaling, intended discussion point. D shows ungridded7×14=98. Multiple answers can have sensible distinguishing reasons; teacher checks and corrects scaling.

Original Activity1 takes place at an art festival. Four original problems: mural15ft×4ft=60 square feet, mosaic12 rows×8 columns of1-inch-square tiles=96 square inches, sidewalk chalk6ft×14ft=84 square feet, sticker pack5 sheets×16 stickers=80 stickers. Learners may be supported to complete at least two problems, but all mathematical source content is mapped.

Source sidewalk poster task: pupils with a partner who used a similar strategy create a visual for the third problem6×14=84; show decomposing14 into10+4 as60+24. Do not mistake area units square feet for sticker counts.

Original Activity2 gallery walk requires pairs to compare poster representations AND leave STICKY NOTES explaining why they agree or disagree. Teacher highlights three different representations of6×14: fully gridded, partitioned/labeled grid, or scaled ungridded area diagram. These are observable collaboration tasks.

Teacher synthesizes strengths and limitations of complete grid, partitioned grid and ungridded source diagrams. Source original five SVGs checked visually; no publisher SVG markup reused. Original gated Find the Area Cool-down and source student PDF not verified. Tests, Stage D and academic signoff deferred.
